title: WHY DO SOME CHRISTIANS NEVER GROW?
paragraphs:
WHY DO SOME CHRISTIANS NEVER GROW?
The frightening possibility is not that you stopped believing in God. It is that you became comfortable knowing about Jesus without allowing Him to change the parts of you that still refuse to surrender.
There is a kind of Christianity that can survive for years without ever becoming mature.
It knows the songs.
It knows when to say “Amen.”
It knows which Bible verses to post when life becomes painful.
It knows how to look faithful in public.
It may attend church, listen to sermons, own several Bibles, follow Christian pages, defend Christian beliefs, and speak fluently about grace.
And yet...
year after year, the same bitterness remains.
The same secret sin keeps returning.
The same unforgiveness controls the heart.
The same pride refuses correction.
The same prayerlessness continues.
The same spiritual excuses survive.
The same wounds become permission to hurt other people.
The same person keeps saying, “God is working on me,” while quietly resisting almost everything through which God intends to change them.
And eventually a terrifying question has to be asked:
Why do some people spend years around Christianity and still seem spiritually unchanged?
Maybe an even harder question is this:
Could that person be me?
Before you answer too quickly, stay here.
Because Scripture gives us something far more uncomfortable than another motivational message about “becoming your best self.”
The Gospel is not self-improvement.
Jesus did not die so that the old you could become slightly more religious.
He died and rose again to reconcile sinners to God, forgive the guilty, give His people new life, and progressively transform those who belong to Him.
And sometimes the greatest obstacle to spiritual growth is not that God has stopped working.
It is that we have learned how to live close enough to Christian truth to feel safe while remaining far enough from surrender that the truth never reaches the rooms we keep locked.
Peter wrote:
“As newborn babes, desire the sincere milk of the word, that ye may grow thereby.”
—1 Peter 2:2, KJV
The Greek text contains this striking expression:
ὡς ἀρτιγέννητα βρέφη... τὸ λογικὸν ἄδολον γάλα ἐπιποθήσατε
Hōs artigennēta brephē... to logikon adolon gala epipothēsate.
The picture is intensely physical.
Newborn babies longing for milk.
Peter's word ἐπιποθήσατε — epipothēsate carries the sense of earnestly longing for or craving something.
Not casually appreciating it.
Not occasionally remembering it.
Craving it.
And ἄδολον — adolon means pure, genuine, unadulterated, without deceit.
Peter's point is beautiful and devastating: believers are to hunger for the nourishment God provides because through it they grow toward maturity in the salvation they have received.
A newborn does not need to be convinced that milk matters.
Hunger tells him.
So perhaps one diagnostic question for the spiritually stagnant Christian is not merely, “How much Scripture do I know?”
It is:
What am I actually hungry for?
Because eventually your appetite reveals what has captured your heart.
You can carry a Bible and hunger for applause.
You can attend church and hunger for status.
You can post Scripture and hunger for validation.
You can sing worship songs and hunger for someone's attention.
You can speak about holiness while secretly feeding lust.
You can talk about forgiveness while replaying someone's offense every night.
You can say that Jesus is enough while spending your entire emotional life trying to prove to strangers that you are enough.
And then Sunday arrives.
You dress the wound.
You hide the addiction.
You silence the questions.
You smile.
Someone asks, “How are you?”
And almost automatically you answer...
“Blessed.”
But inside?
Exhausted.
Dry.
Angry.
Jealous.
Numb.
Secretly ashamed.
Still wrestling with something you promised God six months ago you would surrender.
And perhaps you have begun wondering why Christianity seems alive for everybody else while your own soul feels like it has been standing in the same place for years.
Listen carefully.
Spiritual growth is not measured by how emotional you become during worship.
It is not measured by how many Christian posts you share.
It is not measured by how impressive your theological vocabulary becomes.
It is not measured by how long you have attended church.
Time alone does not produce maturity.
A person can be around Christian things for decades and still require what Hebrews calls “milk” rather than solid food because he has remained immature in understanding and practice.
Paul encountered a similar tragedy in Corinth.
He told believers that he could not address them as spiritually mature but as infants in Christ. Jealousy and strife among them exposed their immaturity.
Think about that.
Their spiritual condition became visible through their relationships.
That means one of the places your spiritual maturity is tested is not merely inside a church building.
It is in your home.
In your marriage.
In the way you speak when angry.
In what happens when somebody corrects you.
In what you do when nobody can see your screen.
In how you treat the person who cannot advance your career.
In whether you secretly celebrate when somebody you envy fails.
In whether you apologize without adding, “but you also...”
In whether you forgive.
In whether you tell the truth when lying would protect your reputation.
In whether Jesus is still Lord when obedience becomes expensive.
That is where theology becomes discipleship.
And this is precisely why spiritual growth can hurt.
Because Jesus loves us too much to merely decorate the person we used to be.
He confronts.
He exposes.
He prunes.
Jesus said:
“I am the vine, ye are the branches.”
Then comes the sentence our self-sufficient hearts hate:
“Without me ye can do nothing.”
—John 15:5, KJV
Nothing.
Christian maturity is not produced by gritting your teeth hard enough.
You cannot manufacture the fruit of the Spirit through personality.
You cannot defeat the flesh through inspirational quotes.
You cannot heal your soul through religious performance.
You cannot become holy while remaining independent of Christ.
The branch lives because it remains connected to the Vine.
This means spiritual growth begins with something our culture deeply dislikes:
dependence.
Jesus, I need You.
Not just when somebody dies.
Not just when money disappears.
Not just when the diagnosis arrives.
Not just when the relationship collapses.
Not just when panic wakes me at 2:17 in the morning.
I need You when everything is going well.
I need You when temptation whispers.
I need You when pride tells me I am right.
I need You when somebody wounds me.
I need You when nobody applauds my obedience.
I need You when Scripture contradicts what I want.
I need You when repentance costs me something.
That is where growth begins to become real.
Paul tells Christians in Romans 12:2:
“Be not conformed to this world: but be ye transformed by the renewing of your mind...”
The Greek is breathtaking:
μεταμορφοῦσθε τῇ ἀνακαινώσει τοῦ νοός
metamorphousthe tē anakainōsei tou noos.
Μεταμορφοῦσθε — metamorphousthe.
Be transformed.
The word describes transformation, a change of form.
And then:
ἀνακαίνωσις — anakainōsis.
Renewal.
Renovation.
A making new.
Christianity is not primarily about teaching an old heart religious manners.
God changes people.
He renews minds.
He reshapes desires.
He teaches His children to hate what destroys them and love what reflects Him.
Yet this transformation does not mean Christians instantly become flawless.
Look carefully at the New Testament and you will never find mature Christianity described as sinless swagger.
Quite the opposite.
Growth often makes a Christian increasingly aware of how desperately he needs grace.
The closer you walk with Christ, the harder it becomes to romanticize the darkness inside yourself.
Things you once excused begin bothering you.
Words you once spoke without conviction begin grieving you.
Pride you once called “confidence” becomes easier to recognize.
Gossip you called “venting” starts looking different.
Lust you called “normal” becomes something you want crucified.
Bitterness you called “protecting my peace” begins revealing its chains.
You start noticing the difference between being sorry that sin produced consequences and being grieved because sin dishonors the God who loves you.
That is growth.
Not perfection.
Direction.
Not pretending you never fall.
Learning where to run when you do.
And the mature Christian increasingly runs toward Jesus instead of away from Him.
This is where shame has deceived countless believers.
You sinned.
Again.
You knew better.
Again.
You prayed about it.
Again.
You promised it was over.
Again.
Then you failed.
Again.
And shame whispered:
“Don't pray now.”
“You're fake.”
“God is tired of you.”
“Hide.”
“Wait until you become better before coming back.”
But that voice does not understand the Gospel.
The Gospel says you were never rescued because you were impressive.
Christ came for sinners.
Jesus carried sin to the cross.
He shed His blood.
He died.
He was buried.
And He rose again.
Your hope has never been the strength of your performance.
Your hope is the sufficiency of Jesus Christ.
That does not make repentance unnecessary.
Grace does exactly the opposite.
Grace teaches us that sin is so serious Christ had to die—and that God's mercy is so astonishing Christ willingly came to save sinners.
So repentance is not paying God back.
Repentance is turning from the poison toward the Physician.
It is finally saying:
Jesus, I cannot keep defending the thing that is destroying me.
I cannot keep calling bondage freedom.
I cannot keep asking You to bless the life I refuse to surrender.
I cannot keep polishing my Christian image while starving my actual soul.
No more hiding.
And maybe that sentence just landed somewhere uncomfortable.
Maybe nobody knows what you are fighting.
Maybe your spouse does not know.
Your pastor does not know.
Your family does not know.
Your Christian friends would never imagine it.
Maybe people look at you and think you are strong.
But God sees the browser history.
God sees the resentment.
God sees the private tears.
God sees the secret relationship.
God sees the jealousy.
God sees the compromises.
God sees what happened.
God sees what was done to you.
God sees what you did.
And still the Gospel announces something scandalously beautiful:
Jesus receives repentant sinners.
This has always been the heartbeat of grace.
Peter denied Him.
David collapsed morally and discovered the agony of repentance.
Thomas doubted.
Paul once persecuted the church.
The woman caught in adultery was publicly humiliated.
The thief beside Jesus was dying under judgment with no lifetime left to repair his reputation.
Again and again Scripture refuses to hide human wreckage.
Why?
Because the Bible is not the story of impressive people climbing their way toward God.
It is the story of the holy God pursuing, redeeming, correcting, forgiving, restoring, and transforming people who desperately need Him.
That is why our message remains:
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the scandal never happened.
Not by renaming sin.
Not by calling evil good.
Jesus does something infinitely greater.
He enters the wreckage and redeems people from it.
The cross does not say your sin did not matter.
The cross reveals how much it mattered.
And the resurrection declares that sin and death do not get the final word over those who belong to Christ.
So why do some Christians never seem to grow?
Sometimes because they consume sermons but rarely obey what they hear.
Sometimes because they want encouragement without correction.
Sometimes because they confuse conviction with condemnation and run from God whenever He exposes something.
Sometimes because they have isolated themselves from meaningful Christian community.
Sometimes because they feed their minds for hours on everything except the things of God.
Sometimes because they have made peace with a sin Jesus is calling them to forsake.
Sometimes because bitterness has become part of their identity.
Sometimes because pride makes correction almost impossible.
Sometimes because they are trying to produce through human effort what can only grow through abiding in Christ and walking by the Holy Spirit.
And sometimes the deepest issue is more fundamental.
Scripture tells us to examine ourselves to see whether we are in the faith.
That should never be weaponized to torment tender believers who genuinely trust Christ and struggle with assurance.
But neither should it be ignored.
Christianity is not merely agreeing that Jesus existed.
It is not inheriting your parents' religion.
It is not baptism without faith.
It is not church attendance without Christ.
It is not Christian vocabulary without conversion.
Jesus calls people to Himself.
To repent.
To believe.
To follow.
And genuine saving faith produces fruit—not flawless fruit, not instant maturity, not identical growth rates, but a life in which God's transforming work becomes increasingly evident.
Maybe your growth feels painfully slow.
Do not confuse slow growth with no growth.
Maybe you still struggle with anger, but now you repent instead of celebrating it.
Growth.
Maybe temptation still comes, but now you fight instead of comfortably feeding it.
Growth.
Maybe forgiveness still hurts, but you are bringing your bitterness to Jesus instead of building your identity around it.
Growth.
Maybe you missed prayer yesterday, but today your heart aches to return.
Growth.
Maybe you still cry over what happened to you, but you no longer believe your wound has the authority to define your future.
Growth.
Maybe you fell again—but this time you stopped making excuses.
Growth.
Fruit grows slowly.
Roots grow where nobody applauds.
And some of God's deepest work happens underground long before anyone else sees the evidence.
So do not despise what Christ is doing merely because it is not dramatic enough for social media.
Stay near Jesus.
Open Scripture when you feel nothing.
Pray when the words come out broken.
Confess sin quickly.
Seek mature believers who will tell you truth instead of merely protecting your feelings.
Belong to a faithful local church where Scripture is taught and Christ is honored.
Receive correction.
Forgive.
Serve when nobody notices.
Give without needing applause.
Turn off what keeps poisoning your mind.
Run from temptation before you feel strong enough to resist it.
Stop negotiating with what Jesus has already told you to surrender.
And when you fail...
run back to Christ.
Again.
And again.
And again.
Not because sin is trivial.
Because His grace is greater than your ability to rescue yourself.
There is another danger we rarely discuss.
You can become addicted to Christian content without becoming devoted to Christ.
Another sermon.
Another reel.
Another devotional.
Another podcast.
Another quote.
Another article.
Another theological argument.
Another emotional worship video.
Consume.
Scroll.
Feel convicted.
Forget it.
Repeat.
Information enters the mind but never reaches the feet.
James warns against hearing the Word without doing it.
Imagine standing in front of a mirror, seeing exactly what needs attention, walking away, and immediately forgetting what you saw.
That is the tragedy of conviction without response.
You can be moved and remain unchanged.
You can cry and remain unchanged.
You can shout “Amen” and remain unchanged.
The question is not whether this article made you feel something.
The question is:
What will you do with what God has shown you?
Maybe tonight the next step is not dramatic.
Maybe it is deleting the number.
Maybe it is confessing the lie.
Maybe it is opening the Bible again.
Maybe it is finally forgiving.
Maybe it is asking someone for help.
Maybe it is returning to church.
Maybe it is admitting that your secret sin has become slavery.
Maybe it is getting on your knees beside your bed and saying the most honest prayer you have prayed in years:
“Jesus, I need You.”
Not eloquent.
Not impressive.
Just true.
If that is you, understand this carefully.
You do not clean yourself up so Jesus will finally want you.
Come to Him.
Repent.
Believe the Gospel.
Receive His mercy.
And let the One who saved you begin changing what you could never change alone.

And if Christ has already been transforming wounds, habits, relationships, desires, or places in your life that once seemed impossible to change, tell somebody what Jesus has done. Your testimony may become the reason another wounded believer realizes there is still hope.
Someone may be one honest encounter with the Gospel away from finally asking for help.
Send this privately to the friend who disappeared from church.
Because there may come a night when the person who needs to read these words again is you.
It does not purchase blessing.
It does not make you more righteous.
It does not earn salvation.
Jesus already paid the price sinners could never pay.
But voluntary generosity can help Gospel ministry reach people.
Supporting this particular ministry is an invitation, never a biblical requirement; Scripture calls Christian giving willing rather than coerced.
Come closer to Jesus.
Because someday your books will remain on a shelf.
Your shirts will fade.
Your mugs will break.
Your followers will forget your posts.
Your achievements will belong to history.
Your body will return to dust.
And none of us will stand before God boasting about how polished our Christian image looked online.
We need Christ.
We need His righteousness.
His mercy.
His blood.
His resurrection.
His grace.
And if you have been spiritually asleep, wake up.
If you have wandered, come home.
If you have sinned, repent.
If you are exhausted, abide in Christ.
If you are ashamed, stop hiding from the Savior who already knows the truth.
If you are growing slowly, keep going.
If you fell yesterday, turn toward Jesus today.
And if you suddenly realized that you have spent years looking Christian while your heart has remained untouched...
do not waste that realization.
Run to Jesus.
Because perhaps the most frightening Christian life is not the visibly scandalous one.
Perhaps it is the life that becomes so comfortable around holy things that it no longer notices it has stopped growing.
And perhaps the greatest scandal of grace is this:
The moment you finally stop pretending you do not need rescuing may become the moment you discover just how far Jesus was willing to go to rescue you.
